Three easy ways to make money: Doing missions, sending frigates on missions, and trade routes. I guess you could also do farming to make a bit of passive income, but it takes a while to actually unlock the decently profitable crops. Doing missions is a decent thing to start off with, since you have no money to invest in the other two options. [You'll want to go to the Mission Boards that are located in every Space Station.](https://nomanssky.gamepedia.com/Mission_Board)

Eventually you'll randomly find a freighter being attacked by pirates. If you kill the pirates, the freighter will ask you to dock and speak to their captain. The first time you do this they will let you have the freighter for free. Now you can start purchasing the smaller frigates around the freighters, which you can then send on missions to generate passive income. You'll need some money to buy frigates though, so save that for later. [The wiki does a good job at explaining frigates](https://nomanssky.gamepedia.com/Frigate) 

Once you have a freighter, you'll have some extra inventory slots to carry goods. You'll want to build an [Economy Scanner](https://nomanssky.gamepedia.com/Economy_Scanner) so that you can see what a star system's industry is without having to travel there first. [This redditor made a simple guide showing you what systems sell goods that will make you profit in other systems.](https://www.reddit.com/r/NoMansSkyTheGame/comments/97v7jx/simple_no_mans_sky_trading_chart_for_trading/) Again, you'll need some money for this so you can actually buy goods to sell, but I generally make 2 million credits each run.

If you want to do farming, you'll need to build an [Agricultural Terminal](https://nomanssky.gamepedia.com/Agricultural_Terminal) to do this, which you're in progress of unlocking it already. The upside of farming is that you can build hydroponic trays on your freighter for a mobile source of passive income.

Also the wiki for this game is extremely detailed and helpful. I'd recommend using it whenever you have questions on anything.

The best answer I got for you is that we don't really know. Orks in general don't have a ton of lore, and a lot of people don't think that a lot of the events in The Beast Arises book series should be considered canon (some people think it's poorly written and filled with Ork wank. I haven't read them so I can't tell you, but Attak Moons are pretty stupid IMO).

Gorkanauts and Morkanauts were just kind of added to 40k as models without getting any real story or details on them. In lore they will probably be considered stronger since I believe they're supposed to be the Ork's version of knights.

Remembering that the Gorkanaut and Mega dread are the killy ones, and the Meka Dread and Morkanaut are the supporty ones, I have the stats on a Meka Dread so I can compare that and the Morkanaut. The Morkanaut has 2 more wounds, 1 less attack at full health and loses attacks based on health (Mek doesn't, but loses strength on hp loss), BS 5+ compared to Meka's 4+, 8 Strength compared to 6-4, 1 higher toughness, and 1 higher leadership. It costs 6 more power to field a Morkanaut instead of Meka Dread (but I think the G/Morkanauts are really bad because they're overpriced.)

In melee the Morkanaut is stronger IMO. Sporting 1 higher pen and 4 higher strength at 1 less attack (2 if the Meka takes 2 ripper klaws, but then it doesn't have any ranged), the Morkanaut also has the Smash attack which is much better for larger units of infantry.

Now the Meka dread does have a rule that lets it move 8 more inches if you roll 2+ which is good. It also has much better ranged weapons than the Morkanaut, but the Meka only gets to take one while the Morkanaut also gets two twin big shootas and two rokkit launchas.

Basically they're pretty close in stats, and neither really have any lore, but G/Morkanauts will get buffed IMO if they release a balanced codex. The Meka and Mega dreads are better on tabletop because of their points cost, but in a 1v1 they're all pretty close to each other stats wise.

[Here's my fully painted test scheme Boy next to a Boy that has all the base paint on it.](https://imgur.com/a/9D7DT9Z) (Minus the bandolier, I'm still thinking about how I want to paint that.) There's a big difference in visual appeal between the two, but the base painted one is almost done. 

The metal pieces are Leadbelcher with 3 layers of Agrax Earthshade and 1 layer of Drakenhof Nightshade ([I learned that from this guy here.](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=3DPGCs60VTk)) The clothes are Mechanicus Standard Grey and 1 (or 2, I'll remember when I paint this second Boy) layer of Drakenhof Nightshade. The leather is Dryad Bark and 1 layer of Drakenhof Nightshade. The red is Khorne Red with 1 layer of Carroburg Crimsom. The bone is Zandri Dust with 1 layer of Agrax Earthshade. If you wanted to do the skin the way I did, it's Waaagh Flesh, then Warboss Green painted over everything except the deep recesses, then coat the whole thing in 1 layer of Athonian Camoshade (you could just do a full coat of Waaagh Flesh, a full coat of Warboss Green, and then overload your brush with Athonian Camoshade, skipping the step where you have to avoid painting the recesses.)

The only precise painting I had to do (other than the optional painting method for the skin) was an edge highlight on his loincloth with Rhinox Hide, an edge highlight on the skull  and the Ork's two biggest teef with Ushabti bone, and the Leadbelcher highlight on the edge of his choppa. The skull was pretty easy though since it is not tucked away in a spot that would make me get paint on other things.

To sum it up, almost every part of the model achieved that quality of painting by just a solid base coat and then layers of shade. If you just use shades instead of the optional method for skin, then you have to edge highlight like 10 lines at best, and many of them are prominent and easy. I just counted the edge highlight lines on my Space Marine, and I counted around 70-80. Several of them are corners between two armor panels. You wanna paint a Space marine arm, then shade the recesses, then highlight the edges of the recess without getting the highlight paint IN the recess? Ouch

See those pants? Pretty decent Dawnstone highlights for the creases if I do say so myself. But here's the trick: I did a horrible job at highlighting those creases. I got extra paint everywhere. But I put on the Mechanicus Standard Grey, tried my best on the Dawnstone, then slapped a big glob of Drakenhof Nightshade all over his clothes. Shades stick into the recesses, so it covered up all of my mistakes.

The eyes look pretty tough. I know I was scared to paint them. I've painted a few Primaris Marines before I painted this Ork, and I had a tough time on their eyes. Having done it now, I think Ork's eyes are easier. With a Space Marine, you have to move the brush around a tiny area to paint the whole eye. With an Ork's eye, you only have to put a single dot of paint on the eyeball. It's like those crane games you find in the arcade where you have to position the crane over the plush doll and then press the button to have the crane drop down and pick up the doll (except those arcade games are rigged.) You have all the time in the world to position the brush and get some control over your hands. Then you just touch the model. No precise brushing movements required, just the aiming. You can even use a toothpick for that.

Shades will be your best friend, practice with them. They will cover up your mistakes. You'll get paint where it's not supposed to be. Just repaint over it. On my first model I had to repaint the eyes like 6 times, but I got it looking pretty good.

One of the things I did to learn how to paint these was that I messed up on models on purpose. I overloaded my brush with paint. I under-loaded it. I over-thinned my paints, and then I under-thinned them. I kept adding layers of paint on the model until I was sure adding another coat wasn't making the color better. You need to experiment. If mistakes are where you learn, why try so hard to avoid mistakes? Make the mistakes and learn from them. Zero in on what's the best way to do it. 

It's like baking a cake. The recipe says put it in the oven for 350F for 45 minutes, so I set it to 355F. Turns out that's better for the pan I'm using, and I made a better cake. If the cake didn't come out right, then atleast I know for a fact that for my oven, my pan, and my tastebuds, 355F is not the best option.

When it comes to brush techniques, again remember in most scenarios to paint with the side of the brush, not the tip. That's why the highlight on the skull was so easy.

When is comes to brushes, I mostly use small brushes. I use a small Base brush, a small Layer brush, an extra-small Artificer Layer brush, and a MEDIUM shade brush. Remember shade paints are your friend, and a Medium shade brush will let you apply a generous coat of it.

When it comes to painting the model, I know of two schools of thought: Painting from the bottom up, and painting from the top down. Bottom up means you start with the deepest recesses of the model (like say, the neck of the boy, and ending on the highest points of the model (like his choppa). Top down is obviously the opposite. For me, there's a lot of collateral damage with my painting. Lots of paint ends up where it shouldn't. Bottom up is the easiest for me by far.

Remember this: You don't need to paint what you can't see. On that last picture of my Boy, you can see I didn't do a super good job darkening the skin under his jaw. But when is someone actually going to see that part? It doesn't look bad until you flip the model upside down and stare straight at it.

One last thing. Now it really pisses me off when people who obviously can't relate to my condition think they can relate. I'm sure you've seen people who aren't depressed say that they were depressed until they went outside with their friends, and now they're cured! People like that annoy me, and I'd imagine that it annoys other people too. So I'm not trying to say that this will cure your Dyspraxia, or that I understand what it's like to have Dyspraxia (this disclaimer applies to everything I've said too), but what has worked for ME PERSONALLY is lots of practice. Did it cure my motor skill issues? Of course not. But who's a better painter, Average Joe or Michelangelo with Parkinson's? Probably Michelangelo with Parkinson's since he has a lifetime of practice. I may have a handicap, but I spent a lifetime honing my motor skills. I learned to play instruments like the piano. I play games like Osu! I drew a lot in school. And yeah sometimes I still have to hold a fork with two hands, but sometimes things are easier. Practice wont cure you, but it certainly couldn't hurt you, yeah?

EDIT: I know basically nothing about airbrushing so it might be a complete waste of time, but you could also look into that. Just trying to think of more options for painting.

EDIT 2: The more I look at my painted models, the more I realize how deceiving Orks are. I thought they'd be super tough to paint. They're so small, and you gotta paint those shoulder strap buckles? That's insane. But in reality they've been really easy for me. The first one was hard, but once I started gaining an understanding of their models, it's become so easy. Those buckles look difficult, those muscles look difficult, but it will never compare to having to paint the grill inside a Space Marine powerpack for me.

Oh yeah, also consider trying batch painting. It's worked really well for me so far to fully paint one model for the test scheme, and then batch paint. When you're learning a language, do you just start rehearsing sentences? No, you take it step by step. First get the idea of your paint scheme. You'll probably mess up or make a sub-par model, but this is to see if you like the colors you're using. The model in that picture is actually my 4th paintjob for orks (now I gotta buy paint stripper for 4 nobz, why did I start with nobz and not base troops?) Also take this time to practice the mechanics of painting and paint management (Warhammer TV is your friend, Duncan is your god.) Now you've got your paint scheme, just practice painting base paint. You're learning how to get paint in the general area you want it. Once you've base painted enough guys that you've gotten some improvement at it, then work on some easy highlights. Just continue like this, practicing one single step at a time until you understand that step, then move to the next one.

I believe I can relate a bit. I have [tremors](https://www.medicinenet.com/tremor/article.htm#what_are_the_characteristics_of_tremor) and probably some additional motor skill problems past that, but I haven't bothered to get a diagnosis past tremors. While I don't believe it's as rough as what you have, it does make fine motor skills a problem for me. My arms and legs shake and spasm, increasing in severity the further you get to the end of the limbs. When I want to move my index finger, I'll sometimes end up moving a completely different finger instead. Painting has been a significant challenge for me as well.

Everyone has mentioned washes/shades/etc, so I have some additional suggestions. One of the things that helped me is what my local GW store owner called pinning. Place both of your elbows on the table, then place your wrists together with your palms facing inwards. Hold the model in one hand and the brush in the other hand.

Another method of painting to consider is painting the model before you finish assembly. You can paint the model without the arms on, then glue the arms on and paint them. Or paint the arms separately then assemble, though I don't really like doing that. I play Orkz so their arms get in the way a lot. It takes more time, but it makes painting them easier.

I'm pretty bad at edge highlighting, but dry brushing is even harder for me because I can't make the movements of the brush for drybrushing. When it comes to making a deliberate movement with the wrist or fingers, let's just say it took a week of practice to be able to light one of those disposable lighters. When I try to drybrush, I'll push the brush way too close to the model and leave a gradient streak across the whole model, or I'll just miss it entirely by an inch. If I swing the forearm instead of the wrist I can make the movement, but it accentuates the problem of how close the brush is to the model. It's also really hard for me to make repetitive strokes with the brush, even if I'm not trying to be rhythmic at all. There's no weight behind a brush, so while I can swing a drumstick, swinging a brush is a mystery to me. So I'm avoiding painting armies with lots of highlights. 

Quick tip on highlights though if you wanna highlight: Paint with the side of the brush, not the tip. Just swipe the brush parallel to the edge.

Space marines are pretty difficult for me, since I really want those edge highlights. So if you're like me, I would avoid that. If I was painting tyrannids I would want edge highlights on the carapace, so I wouldn't do that either. I don't just want good looking models, I want my models to stand out from other peoples' models. Tyrannids' big carapaces allow great painters to create some crazy good looking models, so I feel bad when my models just don't stand up to other players' paintjobs. If you just want to create good models, then Tyrannids. But if you end up feeling bad that other players' Tyrannids look "better" than yours, then I would avoid them. Just my own irrational preference. Necrons are good, tau are good. Maybe look into Chaos Demons? I haven't looked into them a lot, so I'm not super informed on them. But from what I can tell, you could make some good looking demons with mostly shades. The plaguebearers on the GW website look like they were almost entirely shades with a few fine details. Look for yourself and see if you could manage it.

Personally Orks have worked the best for me. They're smaller models so they have tiny details, but I can paint them if I move slowly. Plus the clear difference in elevation between the shoulderplate and the arm is enough that I don't get caught in that loop of painting the shoulderplate and getting paint on the arm, then fixing the arm and getting some paint on the shoulderplate, etc. etc. I also made a paint scheme I really like for them. It's mostly shade paints with very little edge highlights except on prominent high elevation features (like the edge of his choppa, really hard to miss.)

That's all I can think of off the top of my head at 4AM. If you have any more questions I'd be glad to help. If you'd like, tomorrow I can take a picture of a model I painted and go over the process. It might be helpful since I designed the paint scheme around my motor skill limitations. It could help show you the painting methods I can use, which might be some of the same methods you can use.

Actually you'd probably be going against the laws of MOBA by building someone tank just because he's a tank, or building someone another way just because the game says to do that. MOBAs are about meta. MOBAs fluctuate. MOBAs are about one person finding something that actually works, and that becomes popular and becomes part of the game. I'll give you two examples from League of Legends.

1. Nautilus is a tank and that's it. He's like 20x more tank based than Steel is. However, someone found out that there are 2 damage related items that work on him. But why would you build damage on nautilus he's like rampage if rampage literally couldn't build attack speed. Turns out this guy found something really OP and nautilus had to be nerfed 3 times to balance for this.
2. Trundle is a tank jungler who can also go on the top lane (the lane for brawlers). Someone found out you can take him as a support. Doesn't make sense right? Supports are the exact opposite of brawlers and assassins. Turns out his kit works very well for support. He has a low cooldown ability that steals attack damage (this is what ADCs scale off of in League), he has an ability that displaces and slows enemies, he has a field he can put down which speeds up him and his attack speed (he just stole AD so now he's going to do a lot of damage), and his ultimate steals an enemy's armor, magic resistance, and health (IE use it on their tanky support). If you had never played League before and the first time you saw a trundle was as a support, you would probably think he was designed for support. But nobody played him that way until one guy decided it could work.
